summary:
Reporting from 2026 points one way: very few voters are still choosing between the blocs. The election will turn mainly on turnout and on vote shifts inside each bloc. Channel 12/N12 put undecided voters at 10-12% between late July and 9 October. Most of them are torn between parties in the same bloc. Only about 0.6-1.6% of the electorate is undecided between the blocs, roughly 1-2 seats. In N12's 9 October poll, 5% of people who had intended to vote for the Netanyahu bloc said they would switch, against 2% switching the other way. For locality ranking, the persuasion weight should therefore be modest. It should be concentrated where the soft-right and traditional pool is large. Mobilization of reliable change-bloc supporters should carry most of the weight.

Where the soft-right pool sits: Yashar is the main way voters cross over. According to Midgam, 16% of its current voters backed Likud in 2022 and 6% did not vote. Yashar estimates about 200,000 "soft" Likud voters. It is campaigning along the Route 4 suburbs (Kfar Saba, Petah Tikva, Kiryat Ono, Holon, Rishon), in Likud and Shas strongholds in the periphery (Dimona, Kiryat Shmona, Shlomi, Or Yehuda), and among moderate religious Zionists (Gush Etzion, Efrat, Givat Shmuel, Ariel). Yisrael Beytenu has mapped the neighborhoods and polling stations where Likud did best and is concentrating on Russian-speaking ex-Likud voters.

Likud's counter-plan matters for targeting. It is a mobilization drive aimed at low-turnout strongholds, meaning polling stations with about 50% Likud share but only about 35% turnout. Likud internally values this at 2-3 seats and has a stretch goal of 200,000 voters, or 5 seats ("Golden Clusters", run together with Smotrich). Turnout drives that are not targeted in those places would help the Netanyahu bloc. The change bloc should use persuasion there, not generic get-out-the-vote work.

The Haredi vote is unusually uncertain. The UTJ chairman fears lower turnout after the parties failed to pass a draft exemption. A new Haredi Public list is splitting the vote, and Shas is losing traditional voters to Otzma, Likud and Yashar.

Arab sector: the current line-up is a Hadash-Ta'al-Balad Joint List with Ra'am running separately. Statnet links that set-up to roughly 59% turnout. The Konrad Adenauer Program measured 53% in May, before the merger, and actual turnout in 2022 was 53.2%. Crime is by far the top issue there, named by 53-80% depending on the survey. Polls report access barriers for Negev Bedouin, who in some unrecognized villages travel about 50 km to vote, and lower certainty of voting among Arab youth and women. On 23 September the Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify both Arab lists, and that may fuel a backlash vote.

Issues: among Jewish voters, security (39%) and the economy (38%) lead. The draft (34%) and party leader rank high among centrist voters. Among secular youth, the October 7 failures and the inquiry (22%) and the draft (26%) stand out. Undecided Jewish voters say they want unity and less polarization.

Rules that shape field work:
- On 17 September the High Court unanimously barred polling-station staff from reporting to parties which identifiable voters have cast ballots.
- Instead, the committee will publish turnout for every regular polling station at least four times on election day, to all lists at once.
- Intercity buses and trains are free from 20:00 on 26 October.
- Flights bringing expatriates home to vote are capped at the flights already planned, with no transport, lodging or other services of monetary value.

The change bloc's working benchmark for its own strongholds, cited in an N12 analysis column, is above 76% turnout among its supporters in the Sharon, Tel Aviv and Haifa.

Note: the shared web-search budget ran out partway through this desk. Some subtopics were not searched, including Druze and Russian-speaker polls, the parties' field-operation numbers, arrangements for evacuees to vote, and polling on the October 7 commission (see open questions).

findings.topic: Arab-sector polling: turnout and coalition attitudes
findings.claim: A Konrad Adenauer Program (Dayan Center/TAU) survey in May 2026 put expected Arab turnout at about 53% if the lists ran separately, the same as 2022. In that set-up Hadash-Ta'al and Ra'am clear the threshold and Balad does not. A reunited four-party Joint List would lift turnout to about 67%, the highest the program has measured. A large majority backs an Arab party joining the next coalition, and violence inside Arab society is the main reason respondents feel unsafe.
findings.quant: Turnout 53% (separate lists) vs 67% (four-party list, about 16.3 seats). Hadash-Ta'al 5.3, Ra'am 4.6, Balad 1.8 seats. 77.2% support an Arab party in the coalition (43.3% any government, 33.9% centre-left only). 76.9% feel weak personal security; 51.8% cite violence in Arab society as the main reason.
findings.authors: Moshe Dayan Center, Konrad-Adenauer Program for Jewish-Arab Cooperation (TAU)
findings.title: Integration and Influence: Survey of Arab Citizens in Israel
findings.venue: Moshe Dayan Center, Tel Aviv University
findings.relevance: Baseline for Arab-locality turnout potential. Fieldwork predates the August Hadash-Ta'al-Balad merger, so the 53% is a floor for the current line-up. Arab turnout lowers the Netanyahu bloc's seat share and raises Ra'am's kingmaker leverage.

findings.topic: Arab-sector polling: turnout by list configuration (Statnet)
findings.claim: Statnet's Yousef Makladeh links Arab turnout to how the Arab parties run. The configuration actually running in 2026 (a three-party Joint List with Ra'am separate) is associated with about 59% turnout. A full four-party list could reach 67-70%, and four separate lists would leave it below 50%. About 80% of Arab respondents rank crime and violence as their top priority.
findings.quant: Four-party list 67% (70% with a strong campaign), 16-17 seats. Hadash-Ta'al-Balad plus separate Ra'am: about 59% turnout, about 9 seats plus Ra'am 4-5. Configuration resembling June: 55%. All separate: about 48%. Crime ranked first by about 80%; Palestinian issue by 6-8%.
findings.authors: Majd Daniel (reporting Statnet / Yousef Makladeh data)
findings.title: Between 17 seats and the risk of collapse: Statnet polls on Arab party unity (Hebrew)
findings.relevance: Best available scenario-matched turnout prior for Arab localities under the actual 2026 line-up (about 59%). Sample and fieldwork dates were not reported, so treat it as an upper-middle estimate.

findings.topic: Arab-sector turnout drivers and access barriers (Negev)
findings.claim: Experts quoted by Haaretz in June 2026 put Arab turnout at 52-54% with separate lists and 60-63% with a joint list, possibly above 70% with a strong campaign. They named the far right's rise, crime and party unity as the main drivers. Negev Bedouin turnout has fallen from about two-thirds in 1999 to barely above half. Dozens of unrecognized villages have no polling station, and some residents travel about 50 km each way to vote.
findings.quant: 52-54% (separate) / 60-63% (joint) / >70% (joint plus strong campaign), per Dr Samer Swaid. Negev turnout about 67% (1999) vs about 50% (latest). More than 120 crime deaths in 2026 by mid-June. About 50 km travel for some unrecognized-village voters.
findings.authors: Haaretz (Jack Khoury et al.; experts As'ad Ghanem, Doron Navot, Samer Swaid, Taleb el-Sana)
findings.title: From the Jewish Far Right to Violent Crime: What Will Drive Arab Voters in Israel to the Polls?
findings.relevance: Negev Bedouin localities and unrecognized villages have a structural turnout ceiling linked to distance, so transport is the binding constraint there. Gives a campaign-effect range for the model.

findings.topic: Arab youth and women turnout; coalition legitimacy messaging
findings.claim: In August 2026 the Task Force on Arab Citizens of Israel summarized the evidence this way: young Arab citizens expect about 59% turnout, and women are less likely than men to say they will definitely vote. Women and youth are the main upside for raising Arab turnout. Support for an Arab party joining the coalition is highest among Ra'am voters and lowest among non-voters. Campaigns that paint dependence on Arab parties as illegitimate may depress Arab turnout.
findings.quant: Arab youth (18-34) expected turnout about 59%. Support for an Arab party in the coalition: Ra'am voters 95.4%, Hadash-Ta'al 77.2%, Balad 67.6%, Arab voters of Jewish parties 90.6%, non-voters 62.6%.
findings.authors: Task Force on Arab Citizens of Israel
findings.title: Arab Society and Israel's 2026 Elections: Between Electoral Power and Political Influence
findings.venue: Inter-Agency Task Force on Israeli Arab Issues
findings.relevance: Inside Arab localities, the higher-yield groups to mobilize are young people and women. Change-bloc rhetoric about Arab parties affects Arab turnout, which in turn affects the Netanyahu bloc's seat share.

findings.topic: Young voters (18-22): vote, certainty, issues
findings.claim: A Dialog poll of 18-22-year-olds for ynet (5-6 October 2026) finds the youth vote fragmented. Among secular youth, Together, Yashar and the Democrats lead; among religious youth, RZP-Zehut and Otzma lead. Arab youth are far less certain to vote than Jewish youth, and young women are much more often undecided. Security and cost of living top the list of issues, while the draft and the October 7 inquiry mainly move secular youth. Shas collapses among the young, and the new Haredi Public list passes the threshold in this group.
findings.quant: Certain to vote: 67% (all), Jewish 71%, Arab 53%; 19% of Arab youth unsure whether they will vote. Undecided on party 14% (women 20%, men 8%). Secular: Together 20%, Yashar 18%, Democrats 17%. Religious: RZP-Zehut 36%, Otzma 22%. Top issues: security 27%, cost of living 25%. Draft decisive for 26% of secular vs 6% of religious; October 7 inquiry 22% vs 5%. n=543.
findings.authors: Dialog institute for ynet / Yedioth Ahronoth
findings.title: Young voters' seat poll: who is collapsing and who passes the threshold (Hebrew)
findings.relevance: Supports weighting localities with large young secular populations (student towns, Tel Aviv, Haifa, Be'er Sheva, Jerusalem centre) for turnout and draft/October 7 messaging. Arab-youth certainty gap is a turnout-potential input.

findings.topic: First-time Jewish voters
findings.claim: A Midgam poll for N12 (15-22 September 2026) of Jewish first-time voters finds Yashar narrowly ahead of Likud, with 10% undecided. Netanyahu still wins head-to-heads in this cohort, and the cohort leans right. A minority plan to depart from their parents' bloc, mostly towards the change bloc.
findings.quant: About 550,000 first-time voters, roughly 10-12 seats. Yashar 16%, Likud 14%, Together 10%, UTJ 9%, Democrats 7%, RZP 6%, YB 6%, Otzma 5%, Hendel-Zelekha 4%, undecided 10%. 74% right or centre-right. Netanyahu 47 vs Eisenkot 37. 21% expect to vote differently from their parents. n=301, ±4.4.
findings.authors: Midgam (Mano Geva) for N12, reported by The Jerusalem Post
findings.title: First-time Jewish voters could account for up to 12 Knesset seats in upcoming election - poll
findings.relevance: Localities with high shares of first-time voters (young, growing suburbs) are a contested pool. Yashar is the change bloc's strongest vehicle with this cohort.

findings.topic: Undecided pool size and issues (Channel 12, July)
findings.claim: A Channel 12 poll aired 27 July 2026 found about 10% of voters undecided, similar to the same point in 2022, or roughly 8-10 seats in play. Only a small fraction was described as likely to cross between blocs. Cost of living was the top concern of undecided voters, followed by social polarization. (A Channel 12 poll reported by the Times of Israel on 31 July put undecided at 12%, about 600,000 voters.)
findings.quant: About 10% undecided, 8-10 seats. Cross-bloc movers: 1.3% (base unclear). Among undecided: 25% cost of living, 15% polarization. 12% of all respondents say the bloc leader decides their vote; 12% cite personal safety and crime.
findings.authors: Ofer Hadad and Amit Segal, Channel 12 News
findings.title: The 61st seat: who will attract the floating votes? (Hebrew)
findings.relevance: Calibrates the persuasion weight. Most undecided voters are deciding within their bloc. Persuasion messaging to floating voters should centre on cost of living and depolarization.

findings.topic: Undecided pool, cross-bloc switching and October 7 accountability (N12, 9 Oct)
findings.claim: The most recent N12 poll found found has 11% undecided, but only about 5% of them (about 0.6% of all voters) are torn between blocs; the rest are choosing within a bloc. Net switching favours the change bloc: 5% of Netanyahu-bloc intenders now say they will switch, against 2% the other way. Two-thirds say the government has not fixed the October 7 failures, and more voters trust an Eisenkot-led government to fix them.
findings.quant: Undecided 11%. 5.4% of the undecided (about 0.6% of the sample) are between blocs; about 6 seats in play. Switching 5% NB to change vs 2% reverse; 70% unchanged. October 7 failures not corrected: 67% (40% among NB voters). Trust to fix: Eisenkot 48% vs Netanyahu 30%. Bloc vote: anti-Netanyahu incl. Arab parties 50%, NB 35%.
findings.authors: N12 Ulpan Shishi poll (pollster not named in article)
findings.title: 11% still undecided whom to vote for, about 5% don't know which bloc they'll support (Hebrew)
findings.relevance: Strongest evidence that cross-bloc persuasion is worth only about 1 seat. Locality priority should weight turnout and soft-NB defection (October 7 accountability message) over generic persuasion.

findings.topic: Analyst view on what decides 2026: stronghold turnout, threshold, emigrants
findings.claim: An N12 analysis column (8 October 2026) argues the race will be settled by turnout and wasted votes. The change bloc's 'magic number' is above 76% turnout among its supporters in the Sharon, Tel Aviv and Haifa. Likud's risk is supporters staying home, as happened in Likud-leaning cities in September 2019. Several lists sit near the threshold. The column breaks the undecided down by bloc and notes heavy emigration since 2022.
findings.quant: Undecided 10.3% = 2.6% Netanyahu bloc + 1.9% change bloc + 1.6% between blocs + 4.2% other. 2022 threshold 154,855 votes; about 300,000 votes wasted in 2022 (Meretz 3.2%, Balad 2.9%). About 250,000 emigrated in 4 years, fewer than 100,000 returned. Arab turnout 44.6% (2021) to 53.2% (2022).
findings.title: This is what will tip the scales in the election (Hebrew)
findings.relevance: Gives a stronghold turnout target (76%) for the Sharon, Tel Aviv and Haifa. Warns that registered emigrants deflate measured turnout in some localities, so turnout potential should be adjusted for 'phantom' registrants.

findings.topic: Vote-transfer matrix: where each list's 2026 voters came from
findings.claim: A Midgam/N12 poll on 9 September 2026 shows Yashar drawing mostly from Yesh Atid and National Unity voters. It also takes the largest share of ex-Likud voters of any opposition list, plus some 2022 non-voters. Together and Yisrael Beytenu also hold about 12-13% ex-Likud voters. Otzma draws heavily from Shas and first-time voters, and Winter's list draws almost entirely from Likud and RZP/Otzma.
findings.quant: Yashar: Yesh Atid 38%, National Unity 24%, Likud 16%, YB 6%, Labor/Meretz 6%, non-voters 6%. Together: Yesh Atid 44%, NU 18%, Labor/Meretz 13%, Likud 13%. YB: YB 35%, Yesh Atid 22%, NU 13%, Likud 12%, Labor 11%. Otzma: RZP-Otzma 37%, first-time 18%, Shas 15%, Likud 13%. Amcha: RZP-Otzma 48%, Likud 44%. n=504, ±4.4.
findings.authors: Midgam (Mano Geva) for N12 / Ofer Hadad
findings.title: Channel 12 poll: 16% of Eisenkot voters voted Likud in 2022 (Hebrew)
findings.relevance: Use as conversion coefficients. Localities with large 2022 Likud vote and centrist demographics are where Yashar converts. Shas-strong localities are where Otzma gains, which is also relevant to NB internal threshold risk.

findings.topic: Likud 2022 voter retention and reasons for defection
findings.claim: In a May 2026 Midgam/N12 survey of 2022 Likud voters, only 58% said they would definitely vote Likud again. The rest were scattered across Bennett's list, undecided, Yashar, abstention and Yisrael Beytenu. The October 7 failure and the draft were the main reasons for considering a switch. This predates the Bennett-Lapid merger and Yashar's surge, so the split has probably changed.
findings.quant: Definite Likud 58%. Others: Bennett 10%, undecided 8%, Yashar 6%, won't vote 6%, YB 4%, Otzma 3%, Hendel 2%. Reasons: October 7 37%, draft 23%, Netanyahu conduct 14%, division 13%.
findings.authors: Midgam (Mano Geva) / iPanel for N12 Ulpan Shishi
findings.title: The poll that reveals: only 58% sure they will vote Likud again (Hebrew)
findings.relevance: Supports a soft-Likud defection share for Likud-heavy localities. Messaging for those voters is October 7 accountability and the draft or equal burden.

findings.topic: Change-bloc targeting: soft Likud, religious Zionists, Likud-best polling stations
findings.claim: As of early October, opposition parties had informally split the target pools between them. Yashar targets about 200,000 'soft' Likud voters and aims for roughly two more seats from traditional and moderate religious-Zionist voters. It runs a dedicated headquarters under Matan Kahana covering Gush Etzion, Efrat, Givat Shmuel and Ariel. Yisrael Beytenu has mapped the cities, neighbourhoods and polling stations where Likud did best and concentrates there, especially among Russian speakers who voted Likud. Bloc officials saw no significant movement between camps yet.
findings.quant: Soft-Likud pool about 200,000 (a pool, not an expected gain). Yashar goal +2 seats from traditional and religious-Zionist voters; currently about 1-1.5 seats from religious Zionists (internal estimate). Gantz claims internal research shows more than 5 seats' worth of voters want to back Blue and White (unverified).
findings.title: Israel Election 2026: Opposition works to flip Likud, moderate Right voters
findings.relevance: Direct evidence of where the change bloc is already working: Likud-best polling stations, religious-Zionist suburbs and settlement blocs, Russian-speaking ex-Likud areas. The ranking should flag overlap so parties don't duplicate effort.

findings.topic: Yashar geography: Route 4 suburbs
findings.claim: Yashar launched in July as a campaign for the suburban, commuting middle class from northern Sharon to the Shfela (lowlands). Named target areas include Even Yehuda, Kfar Saba, Petah Tikva, Kiryat Ono, Holon and Rishon LeZion. The campaign deliberately avoids Tel Aviv, and its headquarters sits at the Morasha Interchange.
findings.title: Gadi Eisenkot launches a centrist campaign tailored for the commuters of Route 4
findings.relevance: Large, mixed-vote Gush Dan and Sharon suburbs are the core 'swing' localities for within-bloc persuasion and soft-right conversion. They score high on both swing and size.

findings.topic: Shas erosion and traditional voters in the periphery
findings.claim: Shas has fallen from 11 seats to about 7 in polls. Because of the draft crisis it is losing tens of thousands of moderately traditional, working-class voters to Otzma, Likud and Yashar. Eisenkot says he meets would-be Shas defectors in Kiryat Shmona, Shlomi and Or Yehuda. Shas is countering by reconciling Deri with Rabbi Yitzhak Yosef and using religious imagery.
findings.quant: Shas 11 seats (2022) to about 7 in several polls. A Shas activist puts the hard base at about 4 seats.
findings.title: Eisenkot threatens to siphon traditional voters away from a panicking Shas
findings.relevance: Peripheral towns with a large traditional Shas/Likud vote (north, development towns, Or Yehuda type) hold a softening pool. The draft and equal burden is the lever. Flags Shas-heavy localities as swing-relevant.

findings.topic: Yashar field presence in Likud strongholds
findings.claim: Haaretz (July 2026) reports Eisenkot building local campaign structures in deep Likud strongholds. It cites a Dimona gathering run by a local campaign manager, activity in Kiryat Bialik, and a regional manager surprised to find support in such places. The bet is on disillusioned Netanyahu voters.
findings.quant: Dimona event about 40 activists and residents; no volunteer totals published.
findings.title: Inside Likud Territory, Eisenkot Is Quietly Gaining Ground. Will It Be Enough to Defeat Netanyahu?
findings.relevance: Confirms that development-town Likud strongholds are being contested for persuasion. The model should separate persuasion value (positive) from generic turnout value (negative for the change bloc) in such places.

findings.topic: Likud GOTV strategy: low-turnout strongholds
findings.claim: Likud's campaign is concentrating on polling stations where it won about half the vote but turnout was only about 35%. It believes mobilizing stay-home supporters there, including elderly and distant voters, is worth 2-3 seats. On election day it plans to track pre-identified supporters with staff posted near polling places and a backup phone centre. Limits on the Elector app mean it needs more manual ground work.
findings.quant: Target stations: about 50% Likud share, about 35% turnout. Estimated gain 2-3 seats. Likud primary turnout 53.5% (Aug 2026).
findings.title: Benjamin Netanyahu camp divided on Ofer Winter as Likud focuses on turnout mobilization
findings.relevance: Key defensive input. Low-turnout, high-Likud localities are where generic turnout drives would backfire on the change bloc. Our localities' 'turnout upside' must be signed by bloc lean.

findings.topic: Likud-RZP 'Golden Clusters' turnout program
findings.claim: i24NEWS reports a joint Likud and Religious Zionism program, launched with the Binyamin Regional Council head and excluding Otzma. It ranks Likud-stronghold neighbourhoods as 'pure gold', 'gold' or 'silver'; 'pure gold' means lowest turnout combined with high Likud share. The program works through door-to-door canvassing, help reaching polling stations, local key figures and phone banks.
findings.quant: Target 200,000 additional voters, which the party says would bring 5 seats. Four methods: door-to-door, polling-station access help, community key figures, phone calls.
findings.title: Elections 2026: Likud's plan to raise turnout - and the exclusion of Ben Gvir (Hebrew)
findings.relevance: Shows the right is running locality-tiered turnout targeting. Our ranking should identify the same 'gold' areas as defensive priorities (persuasion or demobilization-neutral messaging) rather than turnout targets.

findings.topic: Intra-bloc vote battles (October)
findings.claim: Ynet's 8 October overview describes most of the remaining fight as inside the blocs. Netanyahu is focused on getting Likud voters out in low-turnout places, while Ben Gvir targets young Likud voters. Shas and Otzma fight over traditional voters. In the change bloc, Together is trying to win back former Yesh Atid voters who moved to Yashar. Likud signed a surplus agreement with RZP but not with Otzma.
findings.title: Who vs whom: the 'seat-drinking' battles within the blocs (Hebrew)
findings.relevance: Within-bloc cannibalization (Yashar vs Together and Democrats) does not change bloc totals. Locality scoring for the bloc should not reward zero-sum transfers between change-bloc lists, except to keep marginal lists above the threshold.

findings.topic: Northern confrontation line: Kiryat Shmona mood and baseline
findings.claim: Ynet (August 2026) finds Kiryat Shmona residents feeling abandoned. Some want to break with habit, but the Likud and Shas base remains strong, and residents earlier chose a non-Likud mayor. Likud's share has been falling steadily since 2020. The piece says only about 40% of residents have returned, which conflicts with other reports (see D5-F20).
findings.quant: Kiryat Shmona Likud share: 58.13% (2020) to 51.37% (2021) to 49.47% (2022). 2022: RZP 13.67%, Shas 11%, Zionist opposition combined about 22.6%. About 350 students left, about 100 enrolled.
findings.title: Will Kiryat Shmona vote differently? (Hebrew)
findings.relevance: Northern evacuated towns combine a soft-Likud trend (persuasion value) with depressed home-station turnout from population loss. Adjust turnout baselines, and note that registered-but-absent residents distort locality turnout.

findings.topic: Northern recovery: return rates and returnee profile
findings.claim: More than 60,000 residents within 5 km of the Lebanese border were evacuated. As of September 2026, almost 40% of Kiryat Shmona's roughly 24,000 residents had not returned. Those who returned skew older and poorer, and about half the main-street businesses are closed.
findings.quant: More than 60,000 evacuated. Kiryat Shmona about 24,000 residents, about 40% not returned. About $6 billion earmarked for border communities.
findings.title: In Israel's recovering 'capital of the north,' it's too quiet
findings.relevance: Use a return-rate discount, about 0.6 (range 0.4-0.67 given conflicting reports), on the electorate physically present in confrontation-line towns. The present electorate is older and poorer, so expect lower turnout elasticity and a stronger Likud/Shas base.

findings.topic: Salient issues by segment (IDI Israeli Voice Index, Aug 2026)
findings.claim: IDI's August survey (fieldwork 31 Aug-3 Sep) finds Jewish voters weighting security and cost of living most, followed by the draft and religion and state. Centrist Jewish voters put the economy first and the draft second, the right puts security first, and the left puts religion and state first. Among Arab voters, crime in Arab society dominates. October 7 is central for about two-thirds of Jews but a third of Arabs, and a majority fear domestic interference in the election.
findings.quant: Jews (top-2 factor): security 39%, economy 38%, draft 27%, religion and state 26%, leader 23%, judicial reform 18%. Centre: economy 40.5%, draft 34%, leader 26%, security 25%. Right: security 47%. Left: religion and state 39%. Arabs: crime 53.5%, economy 46%. October 7 central: Jews 68%, Arabs 32%. 59% see a high chance of improper domestic interference. n=755 (605 Hebrew, 150 Arabic), ±3.57.
findings.authors: Viterbi Family Center, Israel Democracy Institute
findings.title: August 2026 survey: 59% see high chance of improper attempts by Israeli political actors to skew election results (Hebrew)
findings.relevance: Message weights per segment: centrist and suburban voters get cost of living plus draft or equal burden, soft right gets security competence, Arab localities get crime and personal security.

findings.topic: Undecided voters want unity; perceived stakes by camp (JPPI)
findings.claim: JPPI's Israeli Society Index (fieldwork 1-3 September 2026, Jewish panel plus Arab sample by Afkar) finds a record share calling this the most important election ever. That view is concentrated on the centre-left and much weaker on the right and among Arabs. Undecided Jewish voters emphasized unity and fewer disputes, unity is the top issue for centrists, and the centre-right is split three ways on prime minister.
findings.quant: 'Most important election ever' 40% (centre-left 60%, left 57%, centre 55%, centre-right 39%, right 35%, Arabs 23%). Centre: unity 30%. Centre-right PM preference: Netanyahu 44%, Eisenkot 21%, Bennett 20%. n=663 Jewish plus 206 Arab.
findings.authors: Jewish People Policy Institute (Madad panel; Afkar Research for Arab sample)
findings.title: JPPI Israeli Society Index - September 2026
findings.relevance: Supports depolarizing, unity-themed persuasion in swing localities. The intensity gap means change-bloc stronghold turnout motivation is high, while the right-wing base is less energized.

findings.topic: Religious-Zionist sector poll
findings.claim: A Dialog poll of national-religious voters (31 Aug-2 Sep 2026) finds the RZP-Zehut list leading with about 30%, ahead of Likud and Otzma. Yashar and Together take only small shares, and 13% are undecided. Security leads as the vote driver, and the draft is the top issue for only 15%.
findings.quant: RZP-Zehut about 30%, Likud 17%, Otzma 12%, Amcha (Winter) 6%, Yashar 4%, Shas 4%, Together 3%, Tropper-Hendel 3%, undecided 13%. Top issue: security 35%, Jewish identity 25%, draft 15%, settlement 14%. n=508/484, ±4.4.
findings.authors: Dialog institute for ynet / Yedioth Ahronoth
findings.title: Election poll: whom the national-religious support - and the draft exemption pushed to the margins (Hebrew)
findings.relevance: Change-bloc conversion potential in religious-Zionist localities and settlements is small (about 7% Yashar plus Together). Treat those localities as low-priority, except for the moderate suburban religious communities Yashar targets.

findings.topic: Haredi turnout risk after the draft crisis
findings.claim: UTJ chairman Yaakov Asher was recorded privately urging activists to bring Haredi voters out. He fears turnout will fall despite four years of demographic growth, citing anger over the failed draft-exemption law, discontent with the leadership, and new Haredi lists.
findings.quant: Asher expects 'tens of thousands' of extra votes from growth if turnout holds; no turnout figures given.
findings.authors: Israel National News (reporting Kan News recordings)
findings.title: UTJ chairman warns of haredi voter turnout drop
findings.relevance: Haredi localities (Bnei Brak, Beitar Illit, Modi'in Illit, El'ad, Jerusalem Haredi neighbourhoods) carry unusual turnout uncertainty and are no-campaign zones for the change bloc. Lower Haredi turnout or a split vote helps the change bloc indirectly. Widen variance there.

findings.topic: Legal: ban on reporting who has voted (High Court)
findings.claim: On 17 September 2026 a unanimous High Court panel (Willner, Stein, Kabub) barred party representatives at polling stations from telling their parties which identifiable voters have cast ballots. It overturned the committee's 6 September permissive decision, holding that election law gives no authority for it and that privacy law forbids it. Parties may still urge people to vote, and campaign software in general is not banned.
findings.quant: Unanimous 3-0. Overturns the CEC decision of 6 Sep 2026; the original ban by chair Sohlberg came on 4 Aug 2026.
findings.title: High Court bars parties from reporting who voted at polling stations ahead of election
findings.relevance: Weakens individual-level knock-and-drag GOTV, which hurts Haredi and Likud machines most. Pre-election voter identification and aggregate polling-station turnout become the main election-day tools.

findings.topic: Legal: CEC publishes polling-station turnout during election day
findings.claim: The Central Elections Committee announced it will publish aggregate turnout for every regular polling station at least four times during election day. The figures go to all lists at once and contain no individual identities.
findings.quant: At least 4 releases on election day; all regular stations; aggregate rates only.
findings.title: Israeli election committee: Parties will see polling station turnout, but not who voted
findings.relevance: Our site should support a live election-day mode. Rank change-bloc-leaning polling stations by gap to expected turnout at each release and send transport and volunteers to them.

findings.topic: Likud plan to use station turnout releases to mobilize
findings.claim: i24NEWS reports that Likud plans to use the committee's election-day station turnout figures to rally its base, by highlighting high turnout in opposition strongholds and Arab communities. This echoes its 2015 'Arabs flocking to the polls' message.
findings.title: Likud revives 'Arabs are flocking to the polls' campaign - this time targeting opposition voters
findings.relevance: Visible surges in change-bloc or Arab stations will trigger right-wing counter-mobilization during the day. Favour quiet, early-day mobilization in our strongholds and avoid public turnout bragging.

findings.topic: Election-day logistics: free intercity transport
findings.claim: The committee declared intercity buses on routes over 15 km and all Israel Railways lines free from 20:00 on 26 October until service ends on election day. Urban buses are not included, and Eilat travel requires advance registration.
findings.quant: Free from 20:00, 26 Oct 2026, to end of service on 27 Oct; intercity routes over 15 km plus all rail.
findings.title: Central Elections Committee declares free public transport on election day
findings.relevance: Helps students and young adults registered at parents' addresses in the periphery travel home to vote. Our turnout-potential metric should up-weight localities with many registered-away young voters reachable by rail or intercity bus.

findings.topic: Expat voter flights and the transport-benefit limit
findings.claim: Fly&Vote and AID aimed to fly 50,000-70,000 Israelis home to vote, and more than 30,000 registered to check eligibility. Israelis abroad cannot vote by post. After Likud petitioned, alleging bribery and a financing breach, the committee chair approved a compromise: no flights beyond those already planned, and no transport, lodging or services of monetary value.
findings.quant: Goal 50,000-70,000; more than 30,000 registered; several thousand paid a $75 fee; about 1 million Israelis abroad.
findings.title: Likud Seeks to Block Initiative to Fly Israelis From Abroad to Vote in Election
findings.relevance: Shows the committee treats organised, funded voter transport and benefits as legally risky. Any change-bloc election-day ride programme needs legal vetting. The expat effect is a small national bump, concentrated in affluent centre-left localities.

findings.topic: Disqualification of Arab lists (potential backlash mobilization)
findings.claim: On 23 September 2026 the Central Elections Committee voted to disqualify the Joint List and Ra'am (18-5 each) and Balad chair Abu Shehadeh (30-4), on petitions led by Likud and the right. The Attorney General opposed the party bans. The High Court was expected to overturn them, and the Joint List called it an attempt to suppress Arab turnout.
findings.quant: Joint List 18-5; Ra'am 18-5; Abu Shehadeh 30-4; Ofer Cassif 19-5.
findings.title: Election panel disqualifies all Arab parties, in move likely to be overturned; Balad leader also barred
findings.relevance: Perceived exclusion has historically energized Arab voters (see Statnet's comments on Ben Gvir and Smotrich as motivation). Shifts the Arab turnout prior slightly upward. Change-bloc parties that backed the Abu Shehadeh ban may face friction in Arab towns.

findings.topic: Neighbourhood-level 2022 baseline (Medlan analysis)
findings.claim: An October 2026 ynet/Medlan analysis of 1,044 urban neighbourhoods (2022 results) finds Likud leading in a majority and Yesh Atid in about a third. The highest turnout was in Haredi neighbourhoods. Some of the lowest measured turnout (central Eilat, Netanya hotel strip) likely reflects registrants who don't live there.
findings.quant: Likud led 552 of 1,044 (max 58.5%, Shazar, Or Akiva); Yesh Atid 355 (max 51.5%, Ramat HaSharon); UTJ 64. Highest turnout 88.1% (Ashdod Zone 7). Low: Me'a She'arim 23.2%, central Eilat 25.7%, Netanya hotel strip 30%.
findings.title: Which neighbourhood is most left-wing, most right-wing, and where do people vote least? (Hebrew)
findings.relevance: Supports sub-locality (neighbourhood or polling-station) targeting inside big mixed cities. Very low turnout often reflects registration artefacts, not mobilizable voters, so cap turnout-upside scores where non-resident registration is likely.

findings.topic: Arab vote for Zionist parties; Democrats' Arab outreach
findings.claim: +972 reports (July 2026) that Ra'am's Mansour Abbas estimates Arab support for Zionist parties at no more than 10-12%. Yair Golan's Democrats are touring Arab towns and expanding Arabic social media, and placed Somaya Bashir (of Jatt) 10th on their list. Killings in Arab communities passed 140 by late June 2026.
findings.quant: Arab vote for Zionist parties about 10-12% (Abbas estimate). More than 140 killed by late June 2026. Joint List won 15 seats in 2020.
findings.title: Palestinians could decide Israel's election. But their parties are at a stalemate
findings.relevance: Within the change bloc, the Democrats are the main list that can win Arab votes directly. Arab localities should be scored for the Democrats separately (direct votes), while for the bloc as a whole their value comes mainly through overall Arab turnout.

parameters.name: arab_turnout_2026_central
parameters.basis: D5-F01: KAP May 2026 measured 53% under the earlier configuration. D5-F02: Statnet ties the actual 2026 line-up (three-party list plus separate Ra'am) to about 59%. D5-F03: Swaid 52-54% separate, 60-63% joint. D5-F05: only 53% of Arab youth are certain to vote. 2022 actual was 53.2%. I shade below 59% because polls tend to overstate turnout (my judgement) and add a small upward nudge for the disqualification backlash (D5-F30).

open_questions: Web search budget (200 calls shared across agents) was exhausted partway through this desk. Not covered: polls on an October 7 state commission, Channel 13/Kan profiles of undecided voters, Gaza-envelope campaigning, and field-operation figures for Together, the Democrats, Yisrael Beytenu, Ra'am and the Joint List. A follow-up run could fill these.
No 2026 poll of Russian-speaking voters was found; the Russian-speaker items surfaced were from 2018 and 2022 and were discarded. Need Statnet, Midgam or Russian-language media subsamples.
No 2026 poll of Druze voters was found. Druze localities (e.g. Daliyat al-Karmel, where Blue and White led in 2022) need modelling from CEC results only.
A Haaretz Hebrew headline seen only in search results said Yashar mapped 40 'target cities', including Hadera, Afula and Dimona. The article is paywalled and was not verified, so the list is unknown.

i24NEWS reportedly showed Likud's share eroding since 2020 in Ramla (48.5% to 39.4%), Akko (39.4% to 32.8%) and Ashdod (36.6% to 28.9%). These figures came only from a search snippet; the page failed to render. Verify against our CEC locality data before use.

Arrangements for evacuated northern and Gaza-envelope residents to vote in the Knesset election (special or out-of-area polling stations) were not found for 2026. The 2024-25 municipal elections used special polling stations nationwide.
Return-rate figures for Kiryat Shmona conflict: CSMonitor says about 40% have not returned, while ynet (Aug 2026) says only about 40% have returned.

The general legal status of party-organised election-day rides for voters was not verified. The CEC's expat-flight compromise suggests funded transport and benefits are legally sensitive; confirm with election-law counsel.
No October 2026 Arab-sector turnout poll (after the disqualification saga and the court's resolution) was found. The latest scenario estimates are from May and June 2026.

Volunteer numbers, GOTV apps and election-day transport plans for change-bloc parties are not in public reporting. Only Likud's plans (station monitoring, phone backup, Golden Clusters) and Yashar's Kahana-led religious-Zionist headquarters were found.
